item.title: Do Large Language Models Think Like Us?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Do Large Language Models Think Like Us?

LLMs produce content that seems human, yet the underlying dynamics differ.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • While LLMs appear to reason, their "thought" processes fundamentally differ from ours.
  • Human reasoning is a kaleidoscope of processes, integrating memory, context, culture, and more.
  • While LLMs can be improved, the underlying dynamics will always be different, according to some.
Source: David Matos / Unsplash

A team of psychologists, computer scientists, and physicists from Italy, Slovenia, and South Korea has proposed seven “fault lines” between human and artificial intelligence (AI). The researchers question the extent to which AI is yielding intelligence, at least in the same form as human intelligence. The authors note the critical shift that occurred between statistical natural language processing (NLP), where AI retrieves and ranks existing information, with the (human) user then able to judge between them, and generative AI, which instead presents one fluent, “authoritative-seeming” answer. In short, while large language models (LLMs) produce content that seems cognitively informed and deliberated, the processes underlying how that content is produced are fundamentally different from human cognition.

One of the fundamental divergences between human and artificial intelligence highlighted by the authors relates to how they use language. AI does not understand language the way a human mind processes it and derives meaning; AI instead recognizes statistical patterns, garnered from human-produced text: “[LLMs] do not track truth conditions or causal structure; they track patterns of co-occurrence, association, and continuation in text.” The authors argue that by supplementing this ability with a number of additional mechanisms such as retrieval-augmented generation, they make LLM outputs look more reliable and more convincing without becoming more knowledgeable.

Examining the differences between human and artificial intelligence, the authors propose seven epistemic fault lines that highlight these differences. These correspond to seven sequential stages of human judgement:

Source: Based on Quattrociocchi et al. (2025)
  • The grounding fault: The authors argue that humans arrive at judgments based on layers of information that are often not accessible to LLMs, such as facial expressions, tone of voice, and social cues. Accordingly, LLMs often underdetect expressions that are sarcastic or ironic, or other human-specific expressions. Despite that, LLMs appear to be getting better at detecting these, though that is related to more effective pretraining and conditioning rather than understanding.
  • The parsing fault: Once humans receive sensory and social information, they begin processing it through simultaneous consideration of meaning and potential responses, while also integrating cultural and social knowledge into determining what is most relevant. LLMs instead tokenize textual information and focus on statistical relationships between tokenized text.
  • The experience fault: Humans and LLMs draw from prior knowledge but in a fundamentally different way. Relying on both physics and psychology, humans draw from episodic memory to recall details that allow us to address new situations. In terms of physics, we can determine (to varying degrees) object permanence, solidity, gravity, and causal forces, while also integrating categories, scripts, and social norms through socialization and culturalization, but also through past experience. LLMs instead rely on statistical patterns or linguistic co-occurrences. Crucially, they do not have episodic or autobiographical memory and have neither intuitive physics nor psychology.
  • The motivation fault: Humans tend to be driven by emotion, motivation, and goals, whereas LLMs are driven by optimization rooted in mechanistic processes. Reinforcement learning with human feedback can adjust the equation for LLMs, but it does not imbue them with the same emotional and goal orientation as humans.
  • The causality fault: Based on these previous processes, humans then reason, by which they infer, integrate, consider counterfactuals, and form causal explanations that can be cognizant of long-term plans. LLMs instead integrate textual context that is devoid of (human) reasoning, relying especially on correlations.
  • The metacognitive fault: Further refining their reasoning, humans evaluate metacognitively, as they consider uncertainties, detect errors, estimate confidence, and consider withholding judgment. This can include integration of social-epistemic norms, taking into account social context and potential reputational costs. According to the authors, LLMs lack metacognition entirely, and this is one of the factors that contributes to hallucinations.
  • The value fault: Human reasoning is thus a kaleidoscope of processes that can integrate personal values, cultural norms, reputational concerns, and goals, while being mindful of consequences for relationships and self-identity. LLMs produce probabilistic, text-based judgments driven by the statistical structure of training data.
article continues after advertisement

The authors’ term—epistemia—describes the phenomenon whereby linguistic plausibility takes precedence over epistemic evaluation. This divergence is consequential, especially as humans increasingly turn to AI for answers to complex problems, as well as intimate psychological problems. The similarity between LLM outputs and human writing is one of the reasons why humans have grown comfortable "talking to" LLMs. Yet, what is going on under the hood is profoundly different. Even as LLMs become more fluent and less prone to obvious errors, this does not, according to this study, mean they are reasoning in the way that humans do.

item.title: The Myth of Testosterone Persists
item.description:
Testosterone

The Myth of Testosterone Persists

This is what happens when pseudo-science dictates public policy.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • The history of studying testosterone is riddled with controversy and misinformation.
  • Testosterone secretions do not occur in social isolation or a vacuum.
  • Public policy should be driven by scientific data, not trends or posturing.

When I introduce my students to the concept of testosterone during our unit on the brain and biology, I generally preface the discussion with some qualifier regarding how referring to this chemical released in our bloodstream as a sex hormone is somewhat misleading. Known as the primary sex hormone in males, misinformation about testosterone has existed for as long as it has been known, going back almost 150 years (Freeman et al., 2001).

Namely, despite being strongly associated with masculinity, technically, both sexes secrete this chemical via their respective sex glands. Additionally, while secretion of testosterone is associated with both sex drive and aggression for men in particular, this is a very simplistic notion of the purpose of this hormone. In fact, testosterone is a critical hormone for the overall health and well-being in males, assisting in such far-reaching functions as immune function, energy levels, and mood regulation. It serves critical functions in women as well, such as contributing to bone density and cognitive functioning, among others.

The Problem With Reducing Body Functions to a Single Hormone

Unfortunately, outside of a holistic approach in understanding the body and its chemical processes, cherry-picking a particular secretion or chemical and assigning it exclusivity regarding specific functions is misleading. Our bodies work as an integrative whole, and the larger endocrine system that secretes hormones is connected to other critical communication systems in our body, such as the nervous system. Testosterone secretions are just one of many chemical secretions that are essential to the overall functionality and health of all sexes. Moreover, it isn't secreted in a vacuum but in tandem with other processes happening in our bodies.

The fundamental disconnect is in taking a chemical process in the body and attempting to assign it to a specific notion of what it means to be a “man”—a concept rooted in social, cultural, and psychological meaning. Many years ago, I wrote a book on the psychology of aggression, dedicating a section specifically to testosterone—which has been linked historically to explanations for aggression (Aalai, 2012). In the past, theories regarding why males in particular were prone to crime tried to link the proclivity to elevated levels of testosterone for those individuals who had some kind of hormonal irregularity—such as an additional Y chromosome, which led to higher-than-regular levels of testosterone in some males’ systems. Of course, such theories were spectacular failures with no scientific merit—again, because aggression, and its relationship to criminality in particular, is a psychological, social, and cultural phenomenon that cannot be reduced down to one specific hormonal secretion or biological process.

The Dynamic Relationship Between Hormones and the Environment

Moreover, many of the ideas regarding linking hormonal levels to behavior fail to take into account the recursive or reciprocal relationship between our bodies and the environment—we do not secrete hormones or engage in bodily processes in isolation. Our bodies respond to what we are exposed to in the environment—be it diet, sunshine, stress, amount of sleep, etc. In other words, hormonal secretions reflect a complex and intricate relationship between bodily processes, environmental exposures, and other factors—such as where we are in the developmental lifespan—which are constantly changing.

article continues after advertisement

It appears that our political leaders have once again popularized the defunct notion of tying levels of testosterone to manliness, or other arbitrary markers of vitality or performance. Last week, the Defense Secretary announced that both male and female members of our military will be assessed and screened regarding their levels of testosterone. The purported purpose? To assure “optimal performance” and “long-term health of warfighters” (as reported by Mitchell, 2026). A fundamental lack of understanding in how our endocrine system works has once again led to reductionistic notions of how to derive meaning from the processes our bodies perform.

Egged on by mis- and disinformation in our increasingly fractured media ecosystem—overrun by influencers and other non-expert figures who have been platformed on social media—it appears military personnel may be the next targets of the pseudoscientific ethos that has come to define our current political moment. While it remains to be seen how documenting testosterone levels of military members will impact perceptions of performance or other professional opportunities, given the extent to which women and other minorities have already been purged from the ranks, it isn’t outside the realm of possibility to consider that those determined to have “low T” may be demoted or receive professional backlash.

This most recent announcement is troubling for many reasons. In addition to being scientifically misinformed, this edict coming out from the Defense Department perhaps best serves as a cautionary tale regarding how public policy can go off the rails when scientific scrutiny is tossed aside in favor of trends and performative posturing.

Copyright Azadeh Aalai 2026

item.title: No, You Don’t Need an ADHD Eval—But You Might Want One
item.description:
ADHD

No, You Don’t Need an ADHD Eval—But You Might Want One

The real value of psychological evaluation for ADHD is differential diagnosis.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • There’s no single gold-standard test for ADHD.
  • Comorbidity is common with ADHD and complicates the diagnostic process.
  • Comprehensive evaluation isn’t always necessary for ADHD, but it’s especially valuable for certain groups.

Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a neurodevelopmental disorder marked by a constellation of inattentive and/or hyperactive/impulsive symptoms. The disorder is presented as a checklist of symptoms that must be present from the developmental period (before age 12 years) and evident across more than one setting (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). The global prevalence for adults with ADHD is 3 percent (Ayano, Tsegay, et al., 2023) and 8 percent for children and adolescents (Ayano, Demelash, et al., 2023).

ADHD is often suspected when a person is having difficulties with managing their attention or impulses. ADHD is also the subject of many social media posts, often with misleading content (Yeung et al., 2022). Accurate diagnosis of ADHD helps individuals find the treatment they need, but what type of provider should someone reach out to for ADHD assessment?

Assessment Practices

The Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders (DSM) does not specify a specific test or method of assessing for ADHD. For children, the most accessible healthcare provider is their primary care provider. Pediatricians are usually the first providers a parent consults with when they have a concern about their child. When a child is struggling behaviorally or academically, a pediatrician may suspect ADHD.

The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has established guidelines for pediatricians regarding the evaluation and diagnosis of ADHD (Wolraich et al., 2019). Pediatricians look for symptoms consistent with the DSM; gather information from parents, teachers, and relevant sources; screen for comorbid conditions; and assist with management of the disorder (Wolraich et al., 2019). Many pediatricians use surveys, such as the NICHQ Vanderbilt ADHD Assessment Scale, to gather data from multiple sources.

The AAP recognizes the challenges in implementing guidelines. Many pediatricians have a limited amount of time they can spend per patient. Gathering additional records from school or therapy providers requires a care management system. An added complication in diagnosis is that symptoms of ADHD overlap with symptoms of other conditions, like anxiety, trauma, and autism.

Since ADHD is not a disorder that requires specific assessment practices, there are different professional opinions on the role of psychology in ADHD assessment. Some argue that pursuing a psychological or neuropsychological evaluation for ADHD diagnosis introduces unnecessary friction in the process. Others point out data supporting a neurocognitive profile common in ADHD and related to executive dysfunction (Pievsky & McGrath, 2018; Wright, 2021). At the end of the day, there is not a gold-standard test or process used to diagnose ADHD.

The value of a psychological evaluation lies in the examination of differential diagnoses and comorbid conditions of ADHD. For younger patients, a comprehensive evaluation can assist with advocating for educational accommodations or modifications.

Differential Diagnoses

Misdiagnosis delays appropriate treatment. It can be confusing to families and patients, and it can erode trust in medical providers. Attention problems are symptoms of many psychiatric conditions, such as anxiety and depression. Children with cognitive or learning problems may look inattentive in a classroom setting. Concentration is very difficult for people with trauma disorders. Impulsivity is seen in behavioral conditions like intermittent explosive disorder and oppositional defiant disorder (ODD). People with medical complications may have changes in their attention functioning consistent with neurocognitive disorder rather than ADHD.

Oftentimes ADHD and autism get misdiagnosed. There is a significant amount of overlap between these two conditions, including social deficits and restricted/repetitive behaviors (Martinez et al., 2024). Careful, comprehensive evaluation can examine the symptoms and help with determining differential or comorbid conditions.

article continues after advertisement

Comorbidity

Because ADHD is a neurodevelopmental disorder, it can frequently co-occur with other neurodevelopmental disorders (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). Neurodevelopmental disorders include intellectual developmental disorder, autism spectrum disorder, developmental language disorder, developmental coordination disorder, specific learning disorder, and other conditions that are present from the developmental period. If you have one of these conditions, you are more likely to have another. Some have stronger relationships than others; ADHD and tics are comorbid, for example, with more than half of children with tics also meeting criteria for ADHD (CDC, 2026).

The most common comorbid conditions include ODD, autism spectrum disorder, personality disorders, and substance use disorders. ODD in particular has a particularly strong relationship with ADHD; approximately half of the people with combined type ADHD also have ODD (American Psychiatric Association, 2022). Psychiatric conditions like anxiety and depression can also co-occur with ADHD. For young children, it is crucial to assess for comorbid learning disorders.

Some comorbid conditions have similar features to ADHD. Patients with autism have difficulty with joint attention, which can result in poor attention to social interactions or shared activities. Attention can be disrupted in anxiety and depression, and these conditions can include symptoms of psychomotor agitation that look like fidgeting. Treating ADHD instead of autism, anxiety, or depression can lead to frustration and prolonged symptoms.

Psychologists and neuropsychologists are trained to assess for a wide range of conditions that may be comorbid with ADHD. Without appropriate assessment of comorbid conditions, treatment can stall.

Benefits of Psychological Assessment

Not only does psychological and neuropsychological assessment help with differential diagnosis and identification of comorbidities, but it also helps with identifying a person’s strengths and weaknesses.

The evaluation process should be rooted in differential assessment. Assessment of intelligence helps define core cognitive ability. Language assessment identifies comorbid developmental language disorder (and, in some cases, difficulties in receptive language due to lapses in attention). Memory assessment can help patients understand the nature of their forgetfulness and help other clinicians identify the difference between a memory and an attention deficit. Academic assessment, particularly in children and adolescents, helps with diagnosing learning problems and understanding how attention and impulsivity relate to academic performance.

article continues after advertisement

ADHD has long been conceptualized as a disorder of executive functioning (Pievsky & McGrath, 2018). Russell Barkley proposed response inhibition as the central executive deficit (Barkley, 1997). Assessment of executive functioning is a key piece of psychological evaluation of ADHD, and psychologists will use a mixture of direct and indirect assessments. Psychologists can help patients understand their executive functioning, including providing recommendations for accommodation or modification.

The Bottom Line

Initial diagnosis of ADHD through primary care is a great way to get access to services and treatment quickly. For those with few complications or other issues, additional evaluation is not necessary. Patients who are younger benefit from comprehensive evaluation for possible comorbidities that can also be impacting educational progress. Patients with any level of symptomology of psychiatric disorders, like depression or anxiety, need a comprehensive evaluation to determine if the impulsivity and attention identified as ADHD are truly ADHD or a pattern of symptoms better explained by a different disorder.

item.title: Is It Self-Care or Self-Surveillance?
item.description:
Body Image

Is It Self-Care or Self-Surveillance?

A routine can soothe us—or turn us into watchers of ourselves.

Posted July 20, 2026

Source: Zephyr_p / Shutterstock

Self-care has become one of the defining ideas of modern life. We are encouraged to protect our sleep, care for our skin, strengthen our bodies, regulate our nervous systems, meditate, hydrate, and track our habits. Much of this is genuinely helpful. A morning walk can clear the mind. Exercise can improve mood. A skincare routine can be soothing.

But practices that begin as care can gradually become another way of scrutinizing ourselves. A fitness tracker becomes a daily judgment. A mirror becomes a place to search for flaws. A wellness routine becomes another list of things we are failing to do correctly. How can we tell when that shift has occurred?

Notice How You Feel Afterward

The same behavior can be caring or critical, depending on the attention we bring to it. Looking in the mirror might help you pause and reconnect with yourself. Or it might send you searching for everything that looks tired, old, uneven, or somehow wrong. Exercise can make you feel strong and alive. It can also become punishment for not looking the way you think you should. A beauty routine may be pleasurable and expressive—or reinforce the belief that your face is a problem to solve before you deserve to be seen. One useful test is how you feel afterward. Do you feel calmer, stronger, or more present? Or do you leave feeling inadequate and newly aware of everything that needs improvement?

When the Body Becomes a Set of Numbers

Psychologists have long studied what happens when people learn to see themselves from an observer’s perspective. Objectification theory describes how girls and women may internalize an outside view of their bodies, leading them to monitor how they appear rather than experience how they feel.

Today, that monitoring extends far beyond the mirror. We can measure our steps, sleep, heart rate, calories, stress, weight, recovery, and productivity. These tools can provide useful information and support healthier habits. But they can also turn the body into something we constantly score and correct. Instead of asking, “Do I feel rested?” we check our sleep data. A low score can make us distrust a perfectly good night’s sleep. A missed exercise goal can feel like failure, even if our body needed rest. The technology itself is not the problem. What matters is whether the information helps you understand yourself or makes you anxious about how you are managing yourself.

Living for an Imagined Audience

We now see ourselves on video calls, examine photographs before posting them, and imagine how we appear entering a room or speaking in a meeting. It's not vanity. We are deeply social, and how others respond to us affects whether we feel accepted and understood. But living with an imagined audience can pull us outside ourselves. “What am I feeling?” becomes “How am I coming across?” “What do I need?” becomes “How do I look?”

article continues after advertisement

This pressure is particularly strong around beauty. Grooming and beauty practices can be creative, pleasurable, and closely tied to identity. Yet they can also become a form of constant correction, with every visible sign of aging treated as a problem requiring intervention. Research suggests that social media can intensify body-image concerns by encouraging us to compare our appearance with other people’s. Over time, those comparisons can shape the standards we use to judge our own bodies.

Often, the real goal is not simply to look better. It's to feel safer being seen. That desire deserves our compassion and understanding. Appearance has a profound effect on how people respond to us. The question is whether our routines help us inhabit our bodies more comfortably—or make us believe we must fix ourselves before entering the world.

Care Is Also an Attitude

Self-care is not only what we do, but how we relate to ourselves while doing it. Research has linked self-compassion with a more positive body image and lower levels of disordered eating. Self-compassion does not require pretending that we love everything about ourselves. It means responding to our perceived flaws with less criticism and more understanding. A workout motivated by care can build strength. The same workout driven by shame can feel like a punishment for not meeting unrealistic standards. From the outside, the two may look identical.

If you are unsure what a routine is doing for you, consider a few questions:

  • Do I feel better afterward, or more dissatisfied with myself?
  • Is this helping me live my life, or making my life smaller?
  • Am I responding to a real need or to an imagined audience?
  • Would I still want to do this if nobody could see the result?

Genuine self-care does not require abandoning fitness, beauty, technology, or personal goals. It simply asks us to notice the relationship we are creating with ourselves. Are your routines helping you feel more at home in your body—or training you to keep watch for what needs fixing?

Copyright 2026, Tara Well, PhD

item.title: Is the Story You Tell Yourself Making You Anxious?
item.description:
Anxiety

Is the Story You Tell Yourself Making You Anxious?

How children’s literature can help kids (and adults) work through worry.

Posted July 20, 2026

Life is not only composed of what happens to us, but is also made up of the stories we tell ourselves about our experiences. Some narratives extract meaning and purpose from life’s most challenging situations, while others lead us to ruminate on the unfortunate, unfair, or unpredictable aspects of life’s events.

By changing our inner narrative to a more balanced, realistic, and empowered point of view, we can become mentally and emotionally resilient. Cognitive behavioral therapy and narrative therapy are approaches that embrace this process of examining the stories we tell ourselves with the goal of restructuring the narrative into a story that supports our growth and well-being.

Telling ourselves an overly negative story often fuels anxiety and depression; however our inner story does not need to go from entirely negative to entirely positive, nor pessimistic to optimistic. In narrative therapy the aim is to avoid being “single-storied,” and instead embrace the richness and complexity of life, leaving room for a wide range of emotions, meanings, and interpretations of our experiences.

Reading books, like Charlotte Agell’s Just for Today, can help children, and their grown-ups, to consider healthier narratives. More than anything, reading books can remind us that our story doesn’t end here—the blank pages ahead offer hope of a satisfying plot twist, an important revelation, and ultimately a happy ending.

Children’s book author and educator Charlotte Agell shares her take on surviving worry spirals and celebrates the life-changing power of reading.

Reading books, like Charlotte Agell’s Just for Today, can help children, and their grown-ups, to consider healthier narratives.
Source: Scholastic/Used with permission

Q: Share a bit about your background and what inspired you to write Just for Today.

Charlotte Agell: I’m a lifelong public schoolteacher and mom, and soon-to-be grandmother. Life is full of love and drama. Just for Today grew out of Elba and Norris’s first adventure, in their debut book, Maybe Tomorrow? They just kept talking to each other, as friends do, and talking to me, telling their stories.

Both Maybe Tomorrow? and Just for Today grew out of things family members said to me. When my daughter was going through a tough time, she said: “Don’t try to fix it, just listen.” I used the character of Norris in Maybe Tomorrow? to teach myself more about that. He’s such a good listener. (It’s funny how characters can be wiser than their creators!)

This new book, Just for Today is about getting caught in a worry spiral and how friends can help each other through that. My mother, who’s very wise, has this saying for when something is so hard it’s almost impossible to imagine anything different. She says, “This is not the end of the story.” I drew on that to explore how the stories we tell ourselves affect our moods and our thinking.

Elba and Norris, like all true friends, hold each other’s stories gently but also prod each other toward growth and calm. This time, Elba can help Norris. I think both books are essentially about the life raft that is deep friendship.

Q: How do the stories we tell ourselves contribute to anxiety? How do the characters in the book decide to try a different story to help with their worries?

article continues after advertisement

Charlotte Agell: Life seems sometimes like a journey of narration. I am from Sweden, but as a child I lived in both Canada and Hong Kong as well, before coming to the U.S. and finding my forever home, Maine. There were a lot of changes, including going to five different schools on three continents between fifth and seventh grade. It was bewildering. I wondered, as one often does, who I was.

I have always been a big reader, someone who has taken solace and inspiration in literature. I have also always been a storyteller. Over the years. I have navigated by story myself. In low moments, I try to reframe my own story. The stories we tell ourselves can sink us or they can help us swim. The right story can make a heart brave. And stories are meant to be shared. That’s what Elba and Norris do, in their own bumbling way, even as the plot thickens and twists and turns.

Q: When the friends get swept away with worry, what helps them find their way back to each other?

Charlotte Agell: Elba, who specializes in worrying, is able to remember what Norris has said: Sometimes, worry is telling yourself the wrong story. Just for today, try telling yourself a different story.” So, she focuses on the moment, not the shipwreck. She notices the butterflies and berries and her own strength. She finds a way to sing about it. Norris, way upriver, has uncharacteristically crumpled. We all do worry, after all. He needs his friend and she shows up for him. And they are both able to go on into the day.

Source: Scholastic/Used with permission

Q: What important lessons about anxiety can young children learn from your book?

Charlotte Agell: I hope that they can learn that worrying is something we all do. When we get carried away by it, it really helps to reach out to someone. Anxiety, of course, is different from worry. I hope that this book, like Maybe Tomorrow? (with its emphasis on grief and loss), can be something like a doorway, an invitation to talk about things. Sometimes, when we read something that resonates, we realize that we do not have to go into hard feelings alone. Children are full of feelings. I hope Just for Today can be a starter kit for exploring worry, one of the harder feelings, with love and reassurance and some humor, too.

article continues after advertisement

Q: What do you hope young readers take away from spending time with Just for Today?

Charlotte Agell: Over the years, my students and my life have taught me a great deal about friendship. At the core, this book is about reaching out, about daring to be yourself with a friend, whether you are happy or sad. Both of these books focus on social-emotional learning, with the characters often taking an opposite perspective on things. I hope that this will invite deep conversation and maybe some hugs and laughter, too.

item.title: The Secret Superpower of Humor in Parenting
item.description:
Humor

The Secret Superpower of Humor in Parenting

Laughter helps shape childhood memories and strengthen family bonds.

Posted July 20, 2026

“One, two, cha, cha, cha… One, two, cha, cha, cha.” My father chanted this as he rhythmically pressed and released the accelerator, causing our massive family sedan to lurch forward and back. My father—a serious physicist who rarely acted silly—was completely out of character, "dancing the cha-cha" while my buddies laughed in the back seat. That playful memory remains etched in what I call my humor happenings—the collection of joyful moments that continue to shape how I see the world.

The Power of Humor in Parenting

Children may not remember every lesson we teach them, but they often remember how we made them feel. One of the simplest ways to create lasting positive memories is through humor.

We've all heard the claim that children laugh hundreds of times a day while adults laugh only a fraction as often. While the exact numbers are uncertain, one truth is clear: children laugh far more than adults. Somewhere between childhood and adulthood, many of us suppress our natural lightheartedness and playfulness. That matters because humor is much more than entertainment. Shared humor strengthens relationships, helps children cope with life's challenges, and creates a family atmosphere where everyone feels safer, closer, and more connected.

Humor is one of parenting's most powerful—and most overlooked—tools. It does far more than make children laugh; it helps shape how they think, feel, relate to others, and ultimately how they navigate life. Over more than four decades of clinical practice, teaching, and research, I have found that healthy humor consistently strengthens children physically, emotionally, cognitively, and socially.

Four Ways Humor Helps Children Thrive

Healthy humor benefits children in four important ways.

  • Laughter, the physical experience of humor, promotes physical and physiological well-being. It reduces stress, encourages relaxation, and can lessen the perception of pain. Children's hospitals increasingly use humor because it helps reduce anxiety, improve cooperation, and make children feel more comfortable with medical providers. A child who laughs is often calmer, more cooperative, and better able to manage stressful experiences.
  • Mirth, the emotional experience of humor, builds resilience. It helps children feel uplifted and delighted while regulating emotions by reducing anxiety and frustration. Children who can laugh through life's smaller setbacks are better prepared for larger ones.
  • Wit, the cognitive experience of humor, encourages flexible thinking by teaching children that there is more than one way to view a situation. Understanding riddles, wordplay, and jokes develops language, creativity, perspective-taking, and problem-solving.
  • Relational fusion, the social bonding experience of humor, builds relationships. Laughing together creates trust, strengthens emotional bonds, increases empathy, and eases tension. Shared laughter becomes an emotional anchor that children often remember long after they have forgotten specific conversations.

Why Humor Strengthens Families

Parents naturally focus on teaching responsibility, respect, and good decision-making. Yet children also need experiences that communicate a simple message: Home is our haven. We enjoy being together. Humor helps create that environment.

A playful comment during a stressful morning, a funny voice at bedtime, or laughing together over a kitchen mishap can instantly change the emotional climate without minimizing the situation. Rather than avoiding serious issues, humor, as a social lubricant, helps families navigate conflict without allowing stress to overwhelm the relationship. Children who feel emotionally connected are generally more willing to cooperate, communicate openly, and recover from conflict.

article continues after advertisement

Parenting is demanding, and humor offers perspective and emotional relief. It reminds us that while raising children is serious work, it is also filled with opportunities for joy.

Five Ways to Bring More Humor into Everyday Parenting

  • Parents do not need to become comedians. Small moments of playfulness—like my father's impromptu "cha-cha-cha"—can have a lifelong impact.
  • Model humor. Children learn by watching us. Parents who laugh, smile, and play naturally encourage children to develop healthy senses of humor.
  • Create a playful environment. Read funny books, tell riddles, invent silly songs, watch age-appropriate comedies, and encourage imaginative play. These experiences help children associate family life with warmth and enjoyment.
  • Celebrate your child's humor. Even predictable jokes deserve appreciation. Encouragement builds confidence, creativity, and communication.
  • Use humor to reduce tension. A playful comment or exaggerated expression can interrupt escalating emotions and make difficult conversations easier.

Teach empathic humor. Humor should leave everyone feeling respected, included, and emotionally safe. Unlike sarcasm or ridicule, empathic humor strengthens relationships rather than weakening them. Help children recognize the difference between humor that connects people and humor that hurts.

The Lasting Gift of Humor

Years from now, your children may not remember every rule you enforced or every lecture you delivered. They are far more likely to remember laughing with you after the pancakes burned, sharing riddles on long car rides, or turning an ordinary day into something joyful.

Those moments may seem ordinary at the time, but they become part of a child's own humor happenings—the joyful memories that quietly shape how they think, feel, and connect with others for the rest of their lives. Humor teaches resilience. It encourages flexible thinking. It strengthens relationships. Most importantly, it reminds children they are loved, accepted, and safe. When lightheartedness becomes woven into family life, everyone benefits. Children grow more confident, emotionally resilient, and socially connected. Parents gain perspective and enjoyment. The relationship between them grows stronger with every shared smile.

Years from now, your children may not remember every rule you made—but they will likely remember your own version of the "cha-cha-cha."

item.title: 5 Things About Panic Attacks I Wish I Had Learned Earlier
item.description:
Anxiety

5 Things About Panic Attacks I Wish I Had Learned Earlier

I recovered from panic attacks. Here are 5 things I wish I'd learned sooner.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Learning about how and why panic happens can help us to gain control over it.
  • Believing in our own safety is breakthrough lesson in coping with panic.
  • Research shows that certain therapeutic interventions can help reduce symptoms of anxiety.

I am 20 years removed from my first panic attack. Panic still arises at times, though it is now much more manageable, and I understand it far better than I did two decades ago. As I reflect on my journey with panic, I can identify five specific concepts that I wish I had learned back when my panic attacks were debilitating and frightening. As a therapist who now treats panic, I consider these five vital points in learning to cope with panic attacks.

5. Panic Attacks Are Not Uncommon

When you are struggling with panic, it can feel extremely isolating, particularly as you notice others around you who are seemingly going through their lives without the constant fear and uncertainty that panic brings. But the reality is that panic attacks are far more common than you might think. According to the Cleveland Clinic, up to 11 percent of Americans experience a panic attack each year, and up to 35 percent will experience a panic attack at least once in their life. My clinical work certainly supports the idea that panic is a common experience: I have seen countless clients who present to therapy reporting struggling with panic. Commonality and shared experience can help to reduce feelings of isolation and alienation that are so often felt when going through panic. Had I known this earlier, I might have placed less shame on myself for struggling.

4. Getting Help Can Help

None of us is immune from the unhelpful belief that we should handle our problems on our own and not burden others, but this line of thinking is particularly unhelpful when coping with panic attacks. Like many young men in their 20s, I initially resisted the idea of getting help for my panic, viewing it as a personal failing to need to outsource what I could do myself—if only I could be stronger and “toughen up.” In retrospect, I recognize that starting therapy was immeasurably helpful to my recovery, and research shows that certain therapeutic interventions, including, but not limited to, cognitive behavioral therapy and panic control treatment, can result in “notable reductions in symptoms of anxiety” (Hansen et al., 2026). It is ongoing work to challenge the narrative of the silent struggle, but it is important that we continue to destigmatize panic.

3. Panic Attacks Are Not Medical Emergencies

I cannot count the number of times I went to the emergency room for what turned out to be a panic attack—but had felt like a heart attack. This is not uncommon among people who experience panic, and the reason is simple, yet something I did not understand at the time: Panic attacks produce “somatic mimics,” physical responses that mimic more serious medical conditions—for example, chest tightness that mimics a heart attack or headaches that mimic an aneurysm. Had I understood this at the time, I might have saved myself a lot of unnecessary trips to the hospital. Panic attacks are uncomfortable, unpleasant, frightening, and sometimes debilitating, but they are not actual medical emergencies, and understanding this can go a long way toward feeling less threatened by them.

article continues after advertisement

2. Small Daily Habits Can Have Big Impacts

This may sound overly simplistic, but I have learned how much daily habits can impact panic attacks. Little, seemingly unimportant things like staying hydrated or moderating caffeine intake have a marked effect on panic. Studies show that worsened sleep quality, increased time spent online, and poor diet can directly affect anxiety and panic (Pedrini et al., 2024). To this day, if I overindulge in coffee, I am likely to experience a jolt of anxiety and panic that I would not have had I been more mindful of my caffeine intake. The lessons of coping with panic attacks are not always big breakthroughs—sometimes they are small and simple, yet no less important.

1. I Was Safe

The first therapist I saw when I was in the throes of panic explained the concept of “fight or flight” and presented panic to me in terms of it being a “primitive response” wherein my mind and body were responding as though I were in immediate danger. This was an absolute breakthrough for me: If I could recognize and even (gulp) accept that I was actually safe despite my body’s uncomfortable somatic mimics, I might be able to feel less at the mercy of panic. Over time, I began to believe in my own safety more and more, and it changed everything. As I felt safer, I was able to step back into a life no longer dictated and restricted by panic. “You are safe” is a big part of the message when I treat clients in my own practice. I wish I had known it earlier. But I am now given the great privilege and responsibility to help others rediscover their sense of safety and learn to live without the constant specter of panic, just as I have.

item.title: 1 Habit That Kills Motivation for Most Adults
item.description:
Motivation

1 Habit That Kills Motivation for Most Adults

Seeking external validation can block internal motivation almost entirely.

Posted July 20, 2026

Key points
  • Chronic external validation seeking flies under the radar because it masquerades as conscientiousness.
  • When approval becomes the fuel, the internal reward system gradually recalibrates.
  • When people are helped to identify and act on their own values and preferences, motivation tends to return.
Source: Nataliya Vaitkevich / Pexels

Motivation rarely disappears after a single bad experience. What erodes it, consistently, is a habit of small surrenders. These are moments where a person defers to the room, waits for a signal, or edits themselves before anyone asks. Repeated often enough, this pattern stops feeling like social awareness and starts feeling like the only way one can function.

The psychological term for what’s happening underneath is externalized regulation, and understanding it explains not just why motivation fades, but why it so often fades in people who are, by any external measure, doing fine.

The Habit of Chronic External Validation-Seeking

The concept comes from self-determination theory, one of the most well-replicated frameworks in motivational psychology. A 2020 review published in Contemporary Educational Psychology, by the theory's originators, synthesizes decades of research showing that lasting motivation requires three conditions:

  1. A sense of competence
  2. A sense of relatedness
  3. A sense of autonomy or the felt experience that your actions are genuinely your own

Chronic external validation-seeking gradually dismantles that third condition. The habit looks harmless, even socially virtuous, in its early forms. You check with your partner before committing to a project. You scan the room before voicing an opinion. You post something and wait, a little tensely, to see how it lands. These moments aren’t inherently problematic. They become a motivation-killer when they calcify into a reflex that says, “I don't act until I know someone approves.”

Why This Habit Hides in a Blindspot

Part of what makes this habit so effective at flying under the radar is that it masquerades as conscientiousness. The person who always runs decisions by others appears thoughtful. The person who holds back an opinion until they’ve gauged the group reads as measured. And in many contexts, including workplaces, families and even certain cultures, these behaviors are actively rewarded.

But there is a difference between consultative decision-making and approval-dependent motivation. In the first, you gather input and then decide, with the locus of commitment sitting inside you. In the second, the decision itself waits to be made by someone else’s reaction, and so does your energy.

A 2021 meta-analysis published in Organizational Psychology Review, drawing on 124 workplace samples, draws a consistent distinction between identified regulation (doing something because it genuinely aligns with your own values) and introjected regulation (doing something to avoid guilt, shame, or the discomfort of disappointing someone).

article continues after advertisement

The latter can produce short bursts of action, but it cannot sustain the kind of intrinsic engagement that feels like real motivation.

How This Habit Hurts the Brain’s Reward System

When approval becomes the fuel, the internal reward system gradually recalibrates. A 2017 peer-reviewed review published in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience found that the brain’s dopamine pathways, which evolved to register effort and progress as intrinsically rewarding, can gradually reorient toward external contingencies over time. In other words, the subtle satisfaction of doing something well stops registering as rewarding, and the brain starts holding out for the response.

This is a learned response that many people develop for sensible reasons like anxious attachment histories, high-pressure environments and workplaces, or families that withheld approval as a form of control. Understanding this can shift the frame: The solution isn’t to care less about people or to become indifferent to feedback. It’s to rebuild the internal signal that existed before the habit of looking outward took hold.

How to Break the Habit and Reclaim Motivation

Research on autonomy-supportive environments, including schools, workplaces, and therapy, offers a consistent finding: When people are helped to identify and act on their own values and preferences, rather than being managed through incentives and evaluations, motivation tends to return on its own. It doesn’t have to be manufactured. It surfaces when approval is no longer the entry fee for action.

One practical entry point is what some psychologists call values clarification, which is a structured process of identifying not what you think you should want but what has historically generated a sense of genuine engagement for you.

A 2015 randomized controlled trial published in Implementation Science found that a structured values clarification exercise promoted more autonomous, internalized motivation in workers compared to a control condition. It also increased the likelihood that they would follow through on their intentions. Not performance, not praise, but the work itself. When people reconnect with even one area where they act from genuine preference rather than expected approval, it can begin to reawaken the broader motivational system.

The other move is deceptively simple: Take small actions that nobody validates. Finish something and tell no one. Make a low-stakes decision without consulting anyone and notice that the world does not end. The point of this simple exercise is recalibration, so that your internal compass that might have fallen into disuse can start functioning properly again.
